description: A fast 2D and 3D game engine — TypeScript SDK, C++/WebAssembly core, visual editor. Ship one project to web, desktop, WeChat MiniGames, playable ads, and native Android / iOS.

latest_release.name: v0.106.0
latest_release.body:
### Added

- **A native build's sockets connect to `wss://`.** `createSocket({ url: 'wss://…' })` now opens on the desktop, iOS and Android runtimes, where it used to report that only `ws://` is supported and close. TLS is the operating system's, as it already is for `fetch`: Network.framework on macOS and iOS, Schannel on Windows, libcurl on Linux and the platform's `SSLSocket` on Android, under the same WebSocket framing a `ws://` connection uses. The certificate chain and the host name are checked against the system's trust store; a connection that fails either reports the reason as an `error` event and closes with 1006. With no port in the URL a `wss://` connection goes to 443. Windows, Linux and macOS were run against trusted, untrusted and wrong-host servers; the Android and iOS code was compiled and has not yet been run on a device.
- **A model's paint can have a clear coat.** A model source's `material` takes `coat` (0 to 1) and `coatRoughness`: a thin glossy layer over what is under it, which is what gives lacquered armour its sharp highlight while the paint below stays as rough as it is.
- **A space frigate example, built from a recipe.** `examples/space-frigate` flies a frigate past a gas giant with no hand-painted texture and no model from another tool: its hull, plating, worn paint, windows, running lights and engines are steps of one model source, baked to a five-thousand-triangle mesh and five 4096 maps; the asteroids it flies through are three more model sources, drifting aft with its speed; the nebula and the planet's bands are generated; the stars are the Starfield effect; the planet's air and the engine plumes are two small shaders. A camera tours six shots on its own, and the keyboard and mouse take it over and work the throttle. One script regenerates every asset, and two more capture frames and check the controls in a headless browser.
- **Stars that stay points.** The new **Starfield** post-process effect draws stars a pixel or two across at any resolution and any field of view, in three layers of brightness, warm and cool, with a band where they crowd (`u_band`, its tilt and turn) and params for density, size and brightness. With `u_sunSize` above 0 it also draws the scene's sun, the first directional light, as a disc of that many degrees with a glow round it (`u_sunGlow`), bright enough for bloom to take. It is added over whatever sky is already drawn, so it goes on top of an environment's panorama: a nebula from an imported HDR keeps its soft cloud and no longer has to hold its stars at the panorama's resolution, where each was a blot several pixels wide. A sky a project writes with `defineSkyEffect` can do the same with `over: true`, and reads `esSkyPixel`, the angle one pixel covers, to size what it draws.
- **A stain can be as fine as the map it is baked into.** A `stain` step given `texel: true` is no longer laid on faces: it is worked out for every texel of the map a `normalBake` with `color` or `surface` writes, over what the faces were painted, in the order the stains are written. Chipped paint, scratches and grime come out at the map's resolution on a model of a dozen faces, where a stain on faces had to split them first and stopped at a million and a half triangles. `where: "edges"` and `where: "cavity"` read the dense surface's shape around each texel, so wear follows a plate's rim and dirt its seam whatever the faces are. With `where` and a `pattern`, `fray` (0 to 1) lets the pattern move the line the shape draws instead of cutting holes in it, which is how paint wears off an edge.
- **Plating for hard surfaces.** The new `panels` step cuts flat faces into plates about `size` across (`uneven` in how they vary, repeatable by `seed`), leaves a `gap` between them, stands each `height` out or sinks it, rounds its top with a `bevel`, and gives the plates `tones` of difference in their paint: a hull, armour, paving. It goes before a `decimate`, and `normalBake` carries it onto the thin mesh.
- *

detail.readme:
# Estella **A 2D and 3D game engine whose editor is an MCP server.**
Your AI agent builds the game with the same 167 tools the editor's own UI uses — then ships it to the web, mini-game platforms, playable ads, desktop and native mobile. [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/esengine/estella)](https://github.com/esengine/estella/releases) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-167_tools-8A2BE2.svg)](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/Platform-Web%20%7C%20Mini--games%20%7C%20Playable%20ads%20%7C%20Desktop%20%7C%20Android%20%7C%20iOS-green.svg)](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/overview/) [![Ask DeepWiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ask-DeepWiki-1f6feb.svg)](https://deepwiki.com/esengine/estella) [Website](https://estellaengine.com)  ·  [Agent](#your-agent-drives-the-editor)  ·  [Getting Started](#getting-started)  ·  [Documentation](#documentation)  ·  [QQ群 481923584](https://qm.qq.com/q/BONa5LXQ0U)
Every frame is one MCP tool call into the editor, captured as it happened — no mouse involved.
## Your agent drives the editor The Estella editor speaks the **Model Context Protocol**. Connect Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client, and the agent works inside the real editor rather than around it: - **It builds** — creates projects, spawns entities from the editor's own Create catalog, writes component fields, makes prefabs, paints tilemaps, writes and type-checks scripts. - **It looks** — takes screenshots of the viewport and the running game, replays a frame draw by draw, compares the game with reference images, and audits what a scene's look lacks. - **It plays** — enters Play mode, steps time deterministically, sends input and clicks UI by name, runs scripted playtests, then reads the running world back. - **It makes assets** — images, sound effects, music and 3D models, each answered with a picture of what it made. - **It ships** — reads project health, exports the game, and drives a build running on a connected phone. Every call goes through the editor's command surface: each one is **one undo step**, you watch it happen in the window, and you can take the mouse back at any time. The editor starts **read-only**; an agent edits only after you allow it in *Window → Connect AI Tools…*, which also writes the client's MCP config for you. | Group | What the agent gets | |---|---| | core | scene tree, entities, components, play / step / input, screenshots, logs, undo | | `assets` · `prefab` · `authoring` | asset documents and import settings, tilemaps, prefabs and variants, physics bodies, UI events | | `look` · `render` | reference images beside the game, light and field sweeps, frame capture and replay, shadows, LOD, bakes | | `code` · `project` | scripts, symbol search, type-check, project settings, health, export | | `image` · `sound` · `modeling` | draw sprites and textures, compose sound and music, build 3D models from steps | | `play` · `view` · `device` | gamepads, time scale, scripted playtests, editor view, and a game running on a connected phone | → [Connecting an agent](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) ## Why Estella, when Unity and Unreal have MCP too? An MCP server can be bolted onto any editor. What an agent can actually get done depends on what sits behind it. - **The protocol is the editor, not a plugin on it.** The 167 tools call the pipelines the editor's own menus, inspector and toolbar run, so an agent's edit is the edit a person would have made, and undoes the same way. Calls are schema-checked and permission-gated by the editor itself. - **The agent can check its own work.** It steps a paused game frame by frame, so "play three seconds, then look" is the same frame every run. It sees the game, not just the log: screenshots, a frame replayed draw call by draw call, the game set beside a reference image, scripted playtests that read the running world back. - **The agent can make what the game needs.** Sprites, textures, sound effects, music and 3D models come from tools inside the editor, so a prototype does not stop at grey boxes while someone opens five other programs. - **Everything is text.** Scenes, prefabs and materials are JSON; gameplay is TypeScript. An agent reads and writes the project directly, and every change is a reviewable diff. - **It ships where heavier engines struggle.** A WebAssembly runtime that loads on a phone browser, seven Chinese mini-game platforms, single-file playable ads for the major ad networks, and native Android / iOS apps — from one project. - **It is open.** The runtime, SDK, pipeline and CLI are Apache-2.0: no royalties, no seats, no runtime fees. The editor is a free download. ## Rendered in real time

One day on the Amazon Lumberyard Bistro, recorded frame by frame from the running game: a sun that follows the clock, weather that turns from clear to mist, rain and snow, baked bounce light, reflections and volumetric haze. Scene © Amazon Lumberyard, CC BY 4.0, modified.

Space Frigate, a game made with Estella and recorded frame by frame as it runs: flying on thrusters, gunnery, and a jump through a gate to another star system. Every model, texture and sound in it is generated from a recipe.
## What's inside Estella is a C++ engine with a TypeScript SDK. The core runs as WebAssembly on the web and natively on desktop and mobile; game logic is written as ECS systems in TypeScript. **2D** — sprites and sprite animation, tilemaps (with LDtk import), Spine 2.1 – 4.3 and DragonBones, 2D lights and shadows, UI with layout, rich and bitmap text, particles, Box2D physics, native 2D rigs. **3D** — glTF / FBX import, PBR materials, directional / point / spot lights with shadows, sky atmosphere with time of day and weather, baked lightmaps, light and reflection probes, SSR, SSGI, height fog, terrain, water, foliage, skeletal animation with spring bones, navigation, Jolt or PhysX physics, streamed large worlds. **Everywhere** — one renderer for 2D and 3D on WebGL 2 and WebGPU, and one project exports to: | Target | What you get | |---|---| | Web | a static, self-contained build | | Mini-games | WeChat, Douyin, Kuaishou, Bilibili, Alipay, Huawei and quick games | | Playable ads | one inlined `index.html` for Meta, Google, Unity, AppLovin, Mintegral, TikTok / Pangle and MRAID networks | | Desktop | a native app on Windows, macOS and Linux — no Chromium | | Android / iOS | a native arm64 app on Vulkan / Metal — not a WebView | ## Getting Started **Install.** Download the editor for Windows or macOS from [estellaengine.com](https://estellaengine.com/#download) — always the newest release. Every build is also on the [releases page](https://github.com/esengine/estella/releases). **Create a project.** Open the editor, click **New Project**, pick a template. **Write a system.** ```typescript import { defineComponent, defineSystem, addSystem, Query, Mut, Res, Time, LocalTransform } from 'esengine'; const Speed = defineComponent('Speed', { value: 200 }); addSystem(defineSystem( [Res(Time), Query(Mut(LocalTransform), Speed)], (time, query) => { for (const [entity, transform, speed] of query) { transform.position.x += speed.value * time.delta; } } )); ``` Press **F5** to play — or connect your agent and ask it to do all three. ## Documentation Everything lives at [estellaengine.com/docs](https://estellaengine.com/docs). | | Start here | What it covers | |---|---|---| | | [Quick Start](https://estellaengine.com/docs/getting-started/quick-start/) | install the editor, make a project, press play | | | [ECS](https://estellaengine.com/docs/core-concepts/ecs/) | components, systems and queries — how game logic is written | | | [AI Agents](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) | connect Claude Code, Cursor or Codex to the editor | | | [Time of Day](https://estellaengine.com/docs/graphics/time-of-day/) | a sun and sky that follow the clock | | | [Weather](https://estellaengine.com/docs/graphics/weather/) | mist, rain and snow | | | [Exporting](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/overview/) | web, desktop, playable ads and the rest, from one project | | | [Mini-game platforms](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/minigame-platforms/) | WeChat, Douyin, Kuaishou, Bilibili, Alipay, Huawei | | | [Android & iOS](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/android-ios/) | native arm64 apps | ## Feedback Estella does not accept pull requests. Bug reports and feature requests are welcome as [issues](https://github.com/esengine/estella/issues) — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for what to include, and for building the engine from source. Maintainers: see the [release procedure](RELEASING.md) for candidate builds, acceptance evidence and publishing. ## License The engine runtime, SDK, asset pipeline, CLI, project templates and editor plugin API in this repository are licensed under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](LICENSE) — free for any purpose, commercial use included. We follow [Semantic Versioning](VERSIONING.md) and keep a [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md). - **The visual editor** is a separate, free product built on this engine; its source is not public. Everything needed to build, run and ship a game is here — see [BUSINESS_MODEL.md](BUSINESS_MODEL.md). - **Trademarks.** The license covers the code, not the "Estella" / "ESEngine" names or logos: say your project uses Estella, but don't ship a fork under that name. - **Spine.** The bundled [Spine Runtimes](third_party) are not open source; a game that uses Estella's Spine integration needs its own Spine license. See [NOTICE](NOTICE).
